episodes.title: A Bank Trained Its Own Foundation Model to Catch Fraud — Freddy Lecue, Wells Fargo
episodes.description:
Freddy Lecue explains how Wells Fargo pre-trained its own transformer from scratch on billions of customer transactions instead of words. The model learns to predict the next transaction, and that one backbone can then be fine-tuned for fraud detection, credit line decisions, anti-money laundering and marketing. He covers the hardest part, turning tabular data like amounts, timing, merchants and zip codes into tokens, plus the model's size and training setup. On fraud, it caught more fraudulent transactions with fewer false alarms than the production XGBoost model, while staying fast enough for real-time card approvals.

episodes.title: How to Let AI Agents Sign Up for Your App Safely — Isabelle Williams, WorkOS
episodes.description:
Isabelle Williams, a product manager at WorkOS, uses a travel app she built to show how to make an app ready for users who arrive as agents. She covers auth.md, an open file that tells agents how to get access; an anonymous mode where an agent can try the app before a person claims its work; and ID-JAG identity assertions, which let the agent's provider vouch for the user so nobody has to fill in a signup form. In a live demo, an agent signs up, plans a trip and books dinner on its own. She then shows how to give an in-app agent its own scoped token so it can be audited, limited and revoked without touching the user's access.

episodes.title: Don't Trust Your AI Agents. Test Them Like a Scientist — Stephanie Jarmak, Omni Analytics
episodes.description:
Stephanie Jarmak, a former astronomer who now builds evals at Omni Analytics after building a large coding benchmark at Sourcegraph, argues that most agent evaluations are easy to misread. She shows how swapping only the harness moved results by 30%, why public benchmarks are for shortlisting rather than decisions, and how to design your own evals like an experiment: realistic tasks, repeated runs, full traces and a measurement that matches what you care about. She also covers quality gates that actually stop work, the human review bottleneck, agent records you can't trust, and why production is the final test.

episodes.title: Why AI Startups Will Disappear Without Compute Markets — Evan Conrad, San Francisco Compute
episodes.description:
Evan Conrad explains how San Francisco Compute, which began as an AI lab that had to sublease its own GPU cluster to stay alive, ended up both operating clusters and running a market for them. He walks through the chain of problems a new lab or inference company hits: everyone is sold out, the deposit eats the bank balance, clusters arrive late and break, and demand is nearly impossible to predict. He argues these are all one risk problem, that AI companies run into credit limits before power limits, and that without a working compute market the price of entry keeps climbing until no new startups can get in.

episodes.title: Better AI Models Won't Fix Your Engineering Team — Nicholas Arcolano, Jellyfish
episodes.description:
Nicholas Arcolano, head of AI and research at Jellyfish, uses data from about 50,000 engineers at 447 companies to ask how much the model really matters for AI coding output. When Cursor pushed many of its users onto Grok, merged PRs barely moved. Breaking down what drives throughput, the tool explains under 1%, skill use about 3% (heavy skill users see roughly a 30% bump), token usage about 9%, company and team about 12%, and the individual engineer most of the rest. The engineers who were top performers before AI are mostly still the top performers now. His advice for leaders: focus on the people, skills and environment you can control.

episodes.title: 1,368 AI Failures and What They Teach About Evals — Vishal Srivastava & Tanmay Sah, New York Life
episodes.description:
Vishal Srivastava and Tanmay Sah studied 1,368 incidents from a public AI incident database to ask what real failures say about how AI systems should be tested. They sort failures across three areas (technical strength, deployment controls and business impact) and 13 sub-areas that cover about 98% of incidents. Weak deployment controls, such as human review and monitoring, are the most closely tied to harm. They show how to rank use cases by how much is at stake, why the evaluator itself needs checking, and a build-break-fix loop that tries to prove a system wrong instead of right, applied to a real airline chatbot that gave a customer the wrong refund policy.

episodes.title: How to Test AI Agents When No Benchmark Exists — Nathanael Weill, Air Canada
episodes.description:
Nathanael Weill leads a team building AI agents at Air Canada, where tasks are so specific there's no public benchmark and domain experts have little time to grade results. His fix is to write the answer first: start from a known answer, generate the input from it, and check whether the agent finds its way back. He shows how that took a past RAG project from one expert-graded test a week to dozens of automated tests a day, then applies it to a supplier-contract review agent with five ways to build a test set: past decisions, planted rule violations, removed clauses, changes that shouldn't matter, and contract templates with filled-in blanks. He also explains why he avoids LLM judges whenever code can check the answer.

episodes.title: Why AI Writing Still Reads Like Slop — Louis-François Bouchard, Towards AI
episodes.description:
Louis-François Bouchard of Towards AI breaks down what makes AI writing feel like slop: overused words, vague generalities, saying nothing, repetition, hallucination and a voice that sounds like everyone at once. He then shows how his team built a benchmark to measure whether a model can write a video script in his own voice: 10 scripts, 5 drafts per model, 4 LLM judges, nine scoring metrics and 1,000 human A/B checks. He shares what it cost, why judges favor their own model family, and practical tips for writing with AI: very long prompts full of examples, one review pass from a strong model, many cheap drafts merged together, and always a human edit.

episodes.title: The AI Content System Behind 200M Views — Sarah Chieng, Cerebras & Cova Lee, OpenAI
episodes.description:
Sarah Chieng (head of developer experience at Cerebras) and Cova Lee (OpenAI developer experience, formerly a full-time creator) share the agent-powered system they use to make content. It runs across six stages: ideating, scripting, recording, editing, repurposing and publishing. Topics include swipe files and custom research tools, voice-based scripting and script skills, shot lists, design systems, and editing through APIs and computer use. They also cover cutting long videos into shorts, scheduled publishing, and a weekly skill that reviews your own process. Their main point: let AI take the tedious work so you can treat content as a craft, not make slop.

episodes.title: Does Code Quality Still Matter? It Depends on This — Max Kanat-Alexander, Capital One
episodes.description:
Every senior engineer's answer is "it depends." Max Kanat-Alexander says what it actually depends on. Code quality always existed for two things: understanding a system and safely changing it. AI is making a new kind of software common: disposable software, with low consequences, few dependents and near-zero cost to replace or maintain. For that software, quality doesn't matter. For durable software it matters more than ever. He also shows how to make systems more disposable and how to make rigor cheap through standards, in-workflow tooling, easy testing and maximum strictness.

- 02:42 Why structure matters
- 04:47 The two risks of every change
